title: Ninety-nine names
hook: the Prophet ﷺ said Allah has ninety-nine names and whoever learns them enters the garden (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-asma' al-husna: the most beautiful names, given for calling. Your line was call him by his names.

A misbaha, a string of Muslim prayer beads, slips through the fingers one bead at a time. Count them and you may find ninety-nine, sometimes split into three groups of thirty-three by two small markers, or thirty-three, meant to go around three times. They hang from taxi mirrors in Cairo and from kitchen hooks in Dearborn. That number isn't random. It comes from a single sentence of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, recorded by both Bukhari and Muslim, with a promise attached. And scholars have turned that sentence over, lovingly, ever since: what the number means, and what it means to know the names.
screen: `PRAYER BEADS IN A TAXI.` → `NINETY-NINE, OR THIRTY-THREE THREE TIMES.` → `ONE SENTENCE, AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, in paraphrase. Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred minus one. Whoever ahsaha them will enter the Garden. And then: He is odd, witr, and He loves what is odd. Everything turns on one verb, ahsaha. At its simplest it means to count, to number off. But the scholars didn't stop at counting. Some said it means to memorize them; others, to understand them; others, to live by them, so that knowing the Merciful makes you merciful, and knowing the Patient makes you patient. Some said a real ahsaha holds all of these. Counting is the door. Living is the house. Then a surprise: the hadith gives the number, but not the list. The list most people learn, sung in schools and printed on posters, comes from a report in Tirmidhi's collection, and hadith scholars such as Ibn Hajar discussed whether a narrator added it rather than the Prophet speaking it. Other early lists differ by a few names. A du'a recorded by Ahmad even asks Allah by every name He has, including names He has kept hidden in His own knowledge. So scholars such as an-Nawawi read the hadith this way: not that Allah has only ninety-nine names, but that ninety-nine come with this promise. Ninety-nine doors, and more behind them. The path takes a first selection, one at a time.
screen: `ONE HUNDRED MINUS ONE.` · `AHSAHA — COUNT, KNOW, LIVE.` · `THE NUMBER, BUT NOT THE LIST.` · `NINETY-NINE, AND MORE BEHIND THEM.` · then, large: `NINETY-NINE DOORS.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the names you already know, saying each one quietly and folding a finger: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim, as-Salam, al-Wadud, al-Hayy, al-Qayyum, maybe al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, or al-Karim, the Generous, from a friend's name. Don't worry about how many. When you run out, rest your hands open and breathe.
Ninety-nine names. The number of names the Prophet said come with the promise of the Garden, for whoever counts, knows and lives by them. Today's word.
Your line: ninety-nine doors. Each name you counted is one you've already found. Day two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims often learn a recited list of the ninety-nine names as children, sometimes set to a melody, and use prayer beads of ninety-nine or thirty-three to remember Allah by His names after prayer.

what it means: ninety-nine names come with a promise for whoever counts, knows and lives by them.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari 7392 and Muslim 2677 give the number only; the Tirmidhi 3507 list is discussed as a possible narrator's addition; Ahmad 3712 speaks of names kept in the unseen.
